newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore economists see brighter export fortunes.
newsitem.headline: Singapore economists see brighter export fortunes.

text.p: Singapore's non-oil exports in May should reinforce views that the trade horizon will brighten in the second half of the year, economists said on Thursday.

A Reuter poll of 10 financial institutions emerged with an average forecast of a 3.5 percent rise in nominal terms for May non-oil exports, a moderately weaker reading than April's actual 5.9 percent.
Improved forecasts came largely from evidence that U.S. orders for electronics, including semiconductors, were on the mend.

But most of the economists, speaking ahead of the announcement of the May figures expected on Friday, said the global pick-up would take at least until July to filter down to local electronic manufacturers.
"The recovery is not so soon. We're still bumping around the bottom for a while," said J.M. Sassoon's Liew Yin Sze. But, he said, inventory cuts were coming to an end.
He cited some spots of weakness in disk drive manufacturing, notably warnings from companies such as Seagate about weaker profit forecasts for the quarter.
Others pointed to bearish estimates from Intel and Maxtor Corp, warning about inventories and sliding prices.
Aggressive production, especially in high-end output, has been leading to inventory excesses, economists said.
Andy Tan of MMS/Standard & Poors qualified his higher 6.5 percent forecast, saying it was partly a factor of low base numbers last year, and not that the recovery was in full blast.
"We've had some profit warnings from Intel, Seagate as well as Cabletron that suggest that demand may slow," Tan said.
These companies had said they would not meet earlier earnings estimates, sending a chill through markets here which produce a major chunk of electronic peripherals.
Tan said a clearer picture of the export trend for Singapore would emerge after looking at June and July levels.
April's non-oil figures had been more bullish than expected after five straight months of decline and some economists said they were still not sure whether it was a one-off.
Prasenjit Basu of UBS Securities said he was guardedly optimistic that negative growth was essentially over.
"It's the beginning of a fairly sustained recovery that should continue through most of the year, with probably some hiccups along the way," he said.

Most economists were slightly bearish on electronics demand, but noted that manufacturers were already pushing for higher output, which was a good sign. A strong positive percentage rise in May would establish a positive three-month moving average.
The Trade Development Board (TDB) said last month it was too early to conclude that an electronics recovery was underway.
It did, however, report that re-exports rose 11.7 percent due to stronger demand for electronics and related products.
Domestic exports to the United States, Singapore's largest trading partner, were up six percent in April after falling 11.4 percent in March, it said.
--Singapore newsroom (65 8703080)
